metaTitle: Ticks in Alberta: Species, Lyme Risk and Season
metaDescription: Alberta's ticks are mostly wood, dog and winter ticks, with no evidence Lyme ticks are established. 2025 data, photos, tick season and what to do.
h1: Ticks in Alberta: Species, Lyme Disease Risk and Tick Season
dek: Which ticks Albertans find, what the province's 2025 tick surveillance found, why its Lyme disease cases are picked up elsewhere, when ticks are active month by month, and what to do with a tick or a bite.
excerpt: Most Alberta ticks are wood ticks, dog ticks and winter ticks. Blacklegged ticks arrive on birds, with no evidence they are established. 2025 data, season, what to do.

quickAnswer.lead: **Yes. Alberta has many ticks, but there is no evidence that blacklegged ticks, the ticks that spread Lyme disease, have established populations there.** Most are Rocky Mountain wood ticks, American dog ticks and winter ticks. In 2025, the province identified 1,332 ticks picked up in Alberta, and 20 of the 100 blacklegged (*Ixodes*) ticks tested carried the Lyme bacterium, [Alberta's tick surveillance dashboard](https://www.alberta.ca/dashboard/tick-surveillance.htm) shows.
bullets: Alberta reported 184 human Lyme disease cases from 1991 to 2023 and says every one was acquired while travelling outside the province; PHAC counted 31 cases in Alberta residents in 2024.
Rocky Mountain wood ticks were the most common of 2,326 ticks removed from people in Alberta and sent to labs from 2000 to 2019, a 2022 study found.
May and June brought 61% of the 5,721 ticks reported to the province from 2022 to 2025, and Alberta says ticks can be active whenever it is above 4 °C.
Alberta's Submit-a-Tick program names a tick from an eTick photo, typically within 2 business days, and its lab tests blacklegged ticks for the Lyme bacterium only.
PHAC's 2025 list of Lyme disease risk areas includes no place in Alberta.

body.text: Are there ticks in Alberta?

Yes, and many kinds. [Alberta's Lyme disease and tick surveillance page](https://www.alberta.ca/lyme-disease-tick-surveillance) says the province is home to many species of ticks and that most of them do not carry *Borrelia burgdorferi*, the bacterium that causes Lyme disease. Some ticks live in Alberta year-round, and migrating birds bring others in from warmer areas each spring.

Most of the ticks people find are wood ticks and dog ticks, plus winter ticks, which live mainly on moose. Ticks that can carry the Lyme bacterium turn up in small numbers: in 2025 the province's [tick surveillance dashboard](https://www.alberta.ca/dashboard/tick-surveillance.htm) counted 167 of them among 1,332 ticks picked up in Alberta, and it says there is no evidence they have formed established populations.

That sets Alberta apart from Manitoba, Ontario and Nova Scotia, where [PHAC](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/ticks-tick-borne-diseases/ticks.html) lists blacklegged ticks as established in at least part of the province. [Our province-by-province guide to ticks and Lyme disease](/learn/ticks-by-province) compares all ten.
Which ticks live in Alberta?

Three *Dermacentor* ticks make up most of what Albertans find. In Alberta Health's [2017 tick surveillance summary](https://open.alberta.ca/publications/2369-0690), American dog ticks, Rocky Mountain wood ticks and winter ticks were two-thirds of the 1,242 ticks from residents who had not travelled in the previous two weeks. Alberta Health's later summaries and the current dashboard group ticks by whether they can carry the Lyme bacterium, not by species.

body.text: PHAC lists the Rocky Mountain wood tick as established in Alberta, British Columbia and some western areas of Saskatchewan, and the University of Saskatchewan's [Western College of Veterinary Medicine](https://wcvm.usask.ca/learnaboutparasites/parasites/dermacentor-andersoni-the-rocky-mountain-wood-tick.php) places it mainly in the southern half of Alberta and British Columbia. Unfed adult females are 5 to 7 mm long and can double in size when fed.

body.alt: Adult female Rocky Mountain wood tick seen from above on a green stem, with a cream-coloured shield behind its head, a dark red body and reddish-brown legs
body.caption: An adult female Rocky Mountain wood tick. The veterinary college describes it as an ornate tick, with white colouring on the shield behind the head.
body.credit: CDC/ Dr. Christopher Paddock; photo: James Gathany (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: These ticks wait on tall grass and low brush along trails, pastures and wooded edges, and the college says they increasingly turn up in urban green spaces such as river valleys, parks and off-leash areas. In 2017, Rocky Mountain wood ticks came mostly from residents of the Calgary (135) and South (101) zones, while American dog ticks came from all five health zones. To tell either from a blacklegged tick, see [our deer tick versus dog tick guide](/blog/deer-tick-vs-dog-tick-canada).

body.alt: Adult female American dog tick on a green blade of grass against a blue background, reddish-brown with a pale mottled shield behind the head and banded legs
body.caption: An adult female American dog tick. PHAC says it, like the Rocky Mountain wood tick, can carry the germs behind Rocky Mountain spotted fever and tularemia.
body.credit: CDC/DVBID/ Gary O. Maupin; photo: James Gathany (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: Which tick bites people most in Alberta?

The Rocky Mountain wood tick. A [2022 study by Alberta laboratory and public health researchers](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8812759/) reviewed 2,326 ticks removed from patients, sent to the province's diagnostic labs from 2000 to 2019 and judged to have been picked up in Alberta. Of these, 1,376 were confirmed Rocky Mountain wood ticks, 410 American dog ticks and 8 winter ticks, while 67 were blacklegged ticks and 11 western blacklegged ticks. The authors note that many ticks are thrown away rather than sent in.
What are winter ticks?

Winter ticks, or moose ticks, spend their whole feeding life on one animal, usually a moose, though they also live on elk and deer. Alberta Environment and Protected Areas' [winter tick fact sheet](https://open.alberta.ca/publications/winter-tick-in-alberta), published in April 2024, says they are common in the foothills and boreal forest and increasingly seen in parkland and prairie. The larvae climb vegetation in late September and early October to catch a passing host and feed through the winter; the province's record is about 140,000 on one moose calf.

body.alt: Adult winter tick seen from above on a white surface, its back covered in a cream and dark brown pattern, with reddish-orange legs
body.caption: A winter tick, or moose tick, photographed in British Columbia.
body.credit: (c) Megan Dark, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist

body.text: The fact sheet says winter ticks very rarely bite humans and are not known to transmit diseases to people. Moose suffer instead: heavily infested animals rub and chew at their coats, leaving large white patches by late winter, and major moose die-offs, which the sheet says seem to occur every 12 to 15 years, have come at times of high tick numbers. [Our winter tick guide](/blog/winter-tick) has more.

body.alt: Moose standing among bare red-stemmed shrubs and dry grass in front of spruce trees, its dark coat broken by large pale grey patches
body.caption: A moose in Edmonton with pale, patchy fur, recorded by the observer on iNaturalist as a sign of winter tick.
body.credit: (c) dalebro, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist

body.text: A few other ticks turn up. Alberta does not test *Ixodes kingi* (114 in 2017), because there is no evidence it can carry or transmit the Lyme bacterium. Brown dog ticks (51 that year) have been reported in Canada in kennels and indoor places with dogs, not in natural outdoor settings, PHAC says, and PHAC lists the lone star tick as found in southern Alberta.
Do ticks in Alberta carry Lyme disease?

A few do. Lyme disease is spread by infected blacklegged ticks and western blacklegged ticks, [PHAC](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/lyme-disease/prevention-lyme-disease.html) says. Alberta counts both species, plus *Ixodes* ticks that cannot be identified further, as ticks able to carry the bacterium, and asks for those ticks to be sent to its lab for testing.

The [dashboard](https://www.alberta.ca/dashboard/tick-surveillance.htm) says there is no evidence these ticks have formed established populations in Alberta and that the ones found were likely brought in on migratory birds or other animals. Field sampling agrees: after *Ixodes* nymphs and adults were submitted in 2017 from hosts that had not left the province, drag sampling near Lethbridge and Vermilion found no *Ixodes* ticks of concern, the [2017 summary](https://open.alberta.ca/publications/2369-0690) reports, and the [2022 study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8812759/) says field sampling from 2014 to 2017 found no blacklegged or western blacklegged ticks. [PHAC's 2025 list of Lyme disease risk areas](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/lyme-disease/prevention-lyme-disease.html), searchable by municipality or postal code, includes no place in Alberta.

body.caption: Percentages are of ticks tested. Before 2021 every tick had to be sent in, so nearly all *Ixodes* ticks were tested; since then photos go to eTick first and only requested ticks reach the lab, and in 2021 testing began only in August. From the summer of 2020, COVID-19 measures stopped submissions from people and the environment, and the dashboard's 2020 counts are all ticks from animals. Submissions are voluntary, so the years are not averaged. Sources: [Alberta's dashboard](https://www.alberta.ca/dashboard/tick-surveillance.htm), data through December 31, 2025; [Alberta Health's 2020 summary](https://open.alberta.ca/publications/2369-0690).

body.text: Keep two numbers apart. Among *Ixodes* ticks tested, 15% to 20% carried the bacterium in eight of the ten years, with 2019 (4.8%) and 2021 (25.8%) the outliers. Among all ticks reported, the share is small: the 20 positive ticks of 2025 were 1.5% of the 1,332 reported. For ticks removed from people, the 2022 study found 8 positives among 76 blacklegged and western blacklegged ticks tested and put the chance that a tick taken off a person in Alberta carried the bacterium at about 0.35%.

*Ixodes* ticks turn up more in the north than in the south. In 2025, they were 48% of the ticks reported from the North Zone (61 of 128) and 41% from the Edmonton Zone (60 of 147), against 3% in the Calgary Zone and under 1% in the South Zone, and most of the year's positive ticks came from the Edmonton (8) and North (6) zones. The dashboard warns that voluntary submissions are not a representative sample of where ticks live.

body.caption: An adult female blacklegged (deer) tick. Of the 167 Lyme-capable *Ixodes* ticks Alberta recorded in 2025, 161 were adults.

body.text: How many Lyme disease cases does Alberta have?

Between 3 and 31 a year since 2011, by PHAC's count. [Alberta's Lyme disease page](https://www.alberta.ca/lyme-disease-tick-surveillance) says all 184 cases reported to the province's Ministry of Health from 1991 to 2023 were acquired while travelling outside Alberta, and it rates the risk of getting Lyme disease from a tick bite in the province as very low. PHAC's [2009 to 2019 review](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/reports-publications/canada-communicable-disease-report-ccdr/monthly-issue/2022-48/issue-5-may-2022/lyme-disease-canada-2009-2019.html) and its annual editions for [2020](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/publications/diseases-conditions/lyme-disease-surveillance-canada-annual-edition-2020.html), [2021](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/publications/diseases-conditions/lyme-disease-surveillance-canada-annual-edition-2021.html) and [2022](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/publications/diseases-conditions/lyme-disease-surveillance-canada-annual-edition-2022.html) also describe Alberta's cases with a known exposure as travel-related.

body.text: The counts swing from 3 in 2020 to 31 in 2024, the highest in this series. When comparing years, keep in mind that PHAC revised the national case definition in 2016 and again in 2024 and says the updates may have affected the data, according to its [Lyme disease monitoring page](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/lyme-disease/surveillance-lyme-disease.html). And because the cases were acquired outside Alberta, the count is not a measure of the risk from Alberta's own ticks.

Nationally, Alberta's 31 cases in 2024 were about half of one per cent of Canada's 5,809, PHAC's [annual report](https://health-infobase.canada.ca/zoonoses/ticks/annual-report.html) shows. Its western neighbours also reported few: British Columbia 21 ([ticks and Lyme disease in British Columbia](/blog/ticks-in-british-columbia)) and Saskatchewan 2 ([ticks in Saskatchewan](/blog/ticks-in-saskatchewan)). For every province's figures, see [Canada's Lyme disease statistics](/lyme-disease-canada-statistics).

body.title: What changed since last year (as of October 2026)
body.text: Alberta's 2025 tick data show 1,332 ticks picked up in the province, down from 1,912 in 2024, but more Lyme-capable *Ixodes* ticks (167, up from 124); 20 of the 100 tested carried the Lyme bacterium, against 13 of 79 in 2024. PHAC had not yet published 2025 Lyme disease counts by province; its preliminary national total for 2025 was 7,105, up from 5,809.
When is tick season in Alberta?

Mainly April to July, with a peak in May and June. Alberta says ticks are most active in spring, summer and fall and can be active when temperatures are above 4 °C, and [PHAC](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/ticks-tick-borne-diseases/ticks.html) adds that ticks can be active whenever it stays above freezing and the ground is free of snow. Our tally of the province's monthly counts shows how lopsided the season is: May and June brought 61% of the 5,721 ticks reported from 2022 to 2025, and April to July brought 84%.

body.text: The season lines up with the temperature. Average daily temperatures in Calgary and Edmonton are close to 4 °C in April and October and below freezing from November to March, according to Environment and Climate Change Canada's 1991–2020 normals for the [Calgary](https://climate.weather.gc.ca/climate_normals/results_1991_2020_e.html?searchType=stnName_1991&txtStationName_1991=Calgary&searchMethod=contains&txtCentralLatMin=0&txtCentralLatSec=0&txtCentralLongMin=0&txtCentralLongSec=0&climate_id=3031092&dispBack=1) and [Edmonton](https://climate.weather.gc.ca/climate_normals/results_1991_2020_e.html?searchType=stnName_1991&txtStationName_1991=Edmonton&searchMethod=contains&txtCentralLatMin=0&txtCentralLatSec=0&txtCentralLongMin=0&txtCentralLongSec=0&climate_id=3012205&dispBack=1) airports. April afternoons average 10.8 °C in Calgary and 10.1 °C in Edmonton.

body.text: Each tick keeps its own calendar. Rocky Mountain wood tick adults peak in May and June and retreat as days turn hot and dry, the veterinary college says, while winter ticks board moose and deer in the fall and stay on them all winter. *Ixodes* ticks show a spring peak and a smaller fall one: of the 100 tested in 2025, 37 were from May and 16 from October. Mosquitoes follow a different calendar; see [when mosquitoes peak in Alberta](/blog/mosquitoes-in-alberta).
How do you get a tick identified or tested in Alberta?

Through the province's Submit-a-Tick program, which starts with a photo. [Alberta](https://www.alberta.ca/lyme-disease-tick-surveillance) asks anyone who finds a tick on a person, a pet or outdoors to consider submitting a photo through eTick's free app or its website. As of October 2026, the steps are:

items: Photograph the tick and submit it through eTick; the species identification typically arrives within 2 business days.
Keep the tick for at least 10 days in a clean, empty plastic container with a tight-fitting lid and no air holes, in case more photos are needed; a fridge or freezer is fine.

If it is a type that can transmit the Lyme bacterium, or cannot be identified from the photo, you will be asked to send it to Alberta Precision Laboratories (APL) with a completed APL Tick Testing Request form, by mail or at a participating lab.
Put one tick in each container, each with its own form and labelled with its eTick ID number, or the lab cannot return results.
APL mails results within 2 to 3 weeks. Ticks of other species can be thrown away.

body.text: APL confirms the species and, where it applies, tests for the Lyme bacterium; testing ticks for other tick-borne diseases is not available in Alberta, and the province says the results are not meant to diagnose or treat illness. Hospital labs and Alberta Health Services Environmental Public Health and First Nations and Inuit Health Branch offices do not accept ticks. APL answers questions about ticks sent to it at 780-407-7121 (press 1), 8 am to 4 pm, Monday to Friday.

[PHAC's tick removal guide](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/ticks-tick-borne-diseases/remove-tick.html) says tick testing is not intended to guide diagnosis or treatment, partly because a person may have been bitten by another tick without noticing and because a health care provider can consider preventive treatment without a tick test. Alberta adds that a provider does not need the tick to make a diagnosis.
What should you do after a tick bite in Alberta?

Remove the tick as soon as you find it. Prompt removal reduces the chance of infection, PHAC says, and Alberta notes that removing a tick within 24 hours of a bite can greatly reduce the chance of Lyme disease or other tick-borne diseases. PHAC's steps:

items: Use clean, fine-point tweezers to grasp the tick's head as close to the skin as possible, and pull slowly straight out.
Try not to twist or squeeze the tick.
If the mouthparts break off, remove them with the tweezers; if they will not come out easily, leave them and let the skin heal.
Wash the bite with soap and water or an alcohol-based sanitizer.

body.text: Do not burn the tick or smother it with nail polish, nail polish remover, essential oils or petroleum jelly; PHAC warns this can make it release its stomach contents, which can be infected, into the bite. In Alberta, keep the tick for Submit-a-Tick; afterwards, PHAC suggests drowning it in rubbing alcohol or freezing it for several days before putting it in the garbage. [Our step-by-step tick removal guide](/blog/how-to-remove-tick-safely) shows the technique.

Then watch your health for a month. Alberta asks anyone with a rash, fever or flu-like symptoms within 30 days of a known tick exposure to tell a health care provider when and where they may have been exposed, and to consult a provider right away if symptoms develop after a bite. Health Link, at 811, can refer callers to a resource that suits their situation.

In most cases an infected tick needs to be attached for at least 24 hours to pass on the Lyme bacterium, [PHAC](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/lyme-disease/prevention-lyme-disease.html) says. Because Alberta's cases were acquired elsewhere, mention recent travel: PHAC lists where you were when bitten among the questions a provider may ask.
What symptoms should you watch for?

Early Lyme disease can bring a rash, fever, chills, fatigue, headache, swollen lymph nodes and muscle and joint aches, [PHAC](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/lyme-disease.html) says. The rash, erythema migrans, is the most commonly reported sign: it typically begins at the bite and slowly grows to more than 5 cm across over several days, may look like a bull's-eye and can go unnoticed on dark skin, and some people do not develop one. Alberta says symptoms can begin 3 to 30 days after a bite.

body.alt: Bull's-eye rash on the back of a person's upper arm above a rolled-up blue sleeve: a dark red centre, a pale ring and a wider red outer ring
body.caption: Erythema migrans, the expanding rash of early Lyme disease, here in its bull's-eye form. PHAC notes that some people do not develop the rash.
body.credit: CDC/ James Gathany; photo: James Gathany (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: Lyme disease is treated with antibiotics, and the earlier the treatment, the greater the chance of a successful recovery, PHAC says. [The stages of Lyme disease symptoms](/blog/lyme-disease-symptoms-guide) covers what can follow if it is not treated.

body.title: See a health care provider if you feel unwell
body.text: Alberta advises consulting a health care provider right away if symptoms develop after a tick bite. This page summarizes what public health agencies publish and is not a diagnosis.
Which other tick-borne diseases occur in Alberta?

A few, rarely. [Alberta](https://www.alberta.ca/lyme-disease-tick-surveillance) lists Rocky Mountain spotted fever (spread by Rocky Mountain wood ticks and American dog ticks), Powassan virus disease (groundhog and blacklegged ticks) and tularemia (American dog ticks), and says the number of these cases reported each year varies from 0 to 3, mainly acquired locally. It adds that there is a low risk that anaplasmosis, babesiosis, ehrlichiosis or southern tick-associated rash illness may occur in the province.

Rocky Mountain wood ticks carry one more risk. Some females produce a toxin in their saliva that causes tick paralysis in pets, livestock and people, seen mainly in central British Columbia, and even one tick can cause a progressive paralysis that can be fatal if it is not found and removed, the [veterinary college](https://wcvm.usask.ca/learnaboutparasites/parasites/dermacentor-andersoni-the-rocky-mountain-wood-tick.php) says. It adds that this tick passes the germs behind Rocky Mountain spotted fever, tularemia and Colorado tick fever to people only very rarely in Canada. [Our Rocky Mountain wood tick guide](/blog/rocky-mountain-wood-tick) has more.

PHAC also links the lone star tick, found in southern Alberta, to tularemia and ehrlichiosis, and says some people bitten by it can develop alpha-gal syndrome, an allergic reaction to red meat from mammals.
How can you avoid tick bites in Alberta?

Dress for ticks, use a repellent that lists them on its label, and check yourself and your pets afterwards. Before going into areas where ticks live, [PHAC](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/ticks-tick-borne-diseases/prevent-tick-bites.html) recommends closed-toe shoes, light-coloured long sleeves and pants, tucking your shirt into your pants and your pants into your socks, permethrin-treated clothing, and a repellent with DEET or icaridin on clothing and exposed skin, following the label. Outdoors, walk on cleared paths and avoid trails made by animals such as deer and moose, since ticks are often found on the grass and plants along them.

Back inside, check yourself, children and gear, shower soon, and put dry clothes in a dryer on high heat for at least 10 minutes; PHAC notes that ticks can survive a cold-warm wash cycle. [Our guide to a full-body tick check](/blog/how-to-do-a-tick-check) shows where ticks hide. Around the home, PHAC suggests mowing often, clearing leaf piles, brush and long grass from the edge of the lawn, and pruning shrubs and trees to let in sunlight.

[Health Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/about-pesticides/insect-repellents.html) caps DEET at 30% for adults and children over 12, and at 10% for children 2 to 12 (up to three times a day) and 6 months to 2 years (once a day), with no DEET for babies under 6 months and no daily use for more than a month in children under 12. Icaridin repels mosquitoes and ticks and should not be used on infants under 6 months. Permethrin-treated clothing can be worn by adults, including pregnant women, but is not available for children under 16. Check that the label lists ticks, since a product that repels mosquitoes might not work on them, and look for the PCP registration number.

Pets can bring ticks into your yard and home, so PHAC advises talking to your veterinarian about tick prevention for them. About half the ticks reported to the province in 2025 came from animals (656 of 1,332), and 91% of those were from household pets, the dashboard shows.

faqs.question: Is there Lyme disease in Alberta?
faqs.answer: Albertans do get Lyme disease, but the province says all 184 cases reported from 1991 to 2023 were acquired while travelling outside Alberta, and PHAC counted 31 cases in Alberta residents in 2024. Blacklegged ticks, which spread the bacterium, turn up in Alberta each year, likely carried in by migrating birds or other animals, and 20 of the 100 tested in 2025 carried it. There is no evidence they have formed established populations, and the province rates the risk of getting Lyme disease from a tick bite in Alberta as very low.

faqs.question: What is the most common tick in Alberta?
faqs.answer: It depends on who finds it. Among ticks removed from people and sent to Alberta labs from 2000 to 2019, the Rocky Mountain wood tick was by far the most common, at 1,376 of 2,326. Among ticks reported by residents in 2017, many of them from pets, American dog ticks (305), Rocky Mountain wood ticks (283) and winter ticks (248) were the top three. Rocky Mountain wood ticks are found mainly in the southern half of the province, and winter ticks live mainly on moose.

faqs.question: When does tick season start in Alberta?
faqs.answer: Usually in April, as the snow melts. Alberta says ticks can be active whenever temperatures are above 4 °C, and average daily temperatures in Calgary and Edmonton reach about that level in April. Reports climb through April and peak in May and June, which together brought 61% of the ticks reported from 2022 to 2025, then drop sharply after July. A smaller rise comes in October, mostly ticks found on animals, and a few ticks are reported in every month.

faqs.question: Can I get a tick tested for Lyme disease in Alberta?
faqs.answer: Sometimes. Alberta's Submit-a-Tick program first identifies the tick from a photo sent through eTick. If it is a type that can carry the Lyme bacterium, or cannot be identified from the photo, you will be asked to send it to Alberta Precision Laboratories with a request form, and the lab mails results within 2 to 3 weeks. The lab tests only for the Lyme bacterium, and the province says the results are not meant to diagnose or treat illness, so see a health care provider if you feel unwell.

faqs.question: Are there ticks in Calgary and Edmonton?
faqs.answer: Yes. Ticks were reported from all five Alberta health zones in 2025, including 260 from the Calgary Zone and 147 from the Edmonton Zone, the provincial dashboard shows, and the University of Saskatchewan's veterinary college says wood ticks are increasingly found in urban green spaces such as river valleys, parks and off-leash areas. In the Edmonton Zone, 41% of the ticks reported in 2025 were Ixodes ticks able to carry the Lyme bacterium, against 3% in the Calgary Zone, though submissions are voluntary and not a representative sample.

faqs.question: Do wood ticks carry Lyme disease?
faqs.answer: No. PHAC names only the blacklegged tick and the western blacklegged tick as spreaders of Lyme disease. Rocky Mountain wood ticks and American dog ticks can carry the germs behind Rocky Mountain spotted fever and tularemia, but Alberta says only 0 to 3 cases of those diseases and Powassan virus disease are reported in the province each year. Winter ticks, the third common tick of this group, very rarely bite people and are not known to spread any disease to them.
